Handling Failures with .NET + Polly: Implementing the Circuit Breaker Pattern
The use of the Polly library to implement smarter failure handling in .NET has been covered multiple times on this blog:
.NET 5 + JWT + Polly + Refit: Consuming secure APIs with simplicity and resilience
.NET 5 + Polly: Improving failure handling with practical examples
In a recent live stream on the Canal .NET channel, I revisited this topic, this time with an example of implementing the pattern known as Circuit Breaker:
Very common in Microservices-based architectures, this pattern involves using an object also called a Circuit Breaker:
•
The Circuit Breaker starts in the Closed status, used to execute code in a protected way while monitoring any failures that may occur;
•
When the number of failures reaches a certain limit within a predefined time interval, the Circuit Breaker transitions from Closed to Open. At this point, attempts to execute instructions with the object representing the circuit will always result in an error;
•
After the aforementioned time period has passed, the Circuit Breaker enters the Half-Open status, where a single execution attempt is made to determine if the circuit returns to the Closed status (the expected behavior for normal situations).
The following diagram summarizes these state changes:
And how does using Polly in .NET fit into all this?
One of the options provided by Polly for implementing the Circuit Breaker pattern is the AsyncCircuitBreakerPolicy type (namespace Polly.CircuitBreaker).
The example I used in the aforementioned live stream is already available on GitHub (I strongly recommend watching the segment that details the Circuit Breaker pattern implementation):
This repository consists of a REST API (APIContagem), along with a Worker Service (WorkerConsumoAPIContagem) that consumes this API and in which a Circuit Breaker was defined using Polly.
In WorkerConsumoAPIContagem, the static CircuitBreaker class was implemented:
•
With CreatePolicy, we create a new Policy based on the AsyncCircuitBreakerPolicy type, specifying in the CircuitBreakerAsync method the maximum number of exceptions before the circuit opens (5 in total), the time it will remain open (10 seconds), and the code for each possible state (parameters onBreak, onReset, and onHalfOpen);
•
The ShowCircuitState method will display information about each state transition.
The object representing the Circuit Breaker (generated via a call to CreatePolicy in CircuitBreaker) **** will be resolved through dependency injection. The instance in question was configured in the Program class, using the AddSingleton method:
In the Worker class, we finally have the usage of the Circuit Breaker:
•
The dependency for this type is resolved in the Worker constructor (lines 22 and 26);
•
The instruction to be executed in a protected way by the Circuit Breaker is on lines 40 and 41.
The following image shows the test project execution. Although failures occurred, the Circuit Breaker does not open (the Closed status remains), and the application recovers from the issues in this simulation:
After successive failures, the circuit opens (Open status), with execution attempts generating exceptions that indicate this status:
